column1: Even after minifying, the browser must:
* parse the JSON into a massive JavaScript object,
* build internal buffers for every vertex,
* keep *all* vertices in RAM (hundreds of MB).
That is why the tab hangs or dies. The only reliable fix is to **serve only the data that is actually needed for the current view**, which is exactly what tiled formats do.

What's the best pipeline to merge OpenStreetMap data with my polygons and build that combined tileset?
,**Short answer – don’t do it unless you really need a single-file, offline-only map.**
In virtually every production web-app the best practice is **“basemap + your data = two sources.”**

MapLibre can request a vector-tile basemap and a separate vector (or GeoJSON) source in the same style with no extra cost – the browser opens two HTTP connections in parallel and composites the layers in draw order.

If you still need a *single* combined tileset (e.g. an air-gapped kiosk, a demo that must ship one MBTiles/PMTiles file, or a client that forbids multiple URLs), the pipeline below will get you there. I’ll also point out the trade-offs so you can decide whether it’s worth the extra work.
## 1️⃣ Why the “two-source” pattern is usually better

column4: Single combined tileset

column3: Browsers download only the tiles they need from each source; each source can be cached independently.
column4: One larger tile set → larger per-tile payload (you lose the “only-what-you-see” advantage of vector tiles).

column3: You can query your own source (`map.queryRenderedFeatures`) without touching the basemap.
column4: Same, but you lose the ability to turn the basemap on/off or style it differently without rebuilding.

column3: Details
Vector tile URLs and the style JSON must allow cross-origin requests from your domain (or you must serve them from the same origin).

The style JSON usually contains an `attribution` field. The plugin does **not** automatically add it to Leaflet’s control; you should add it manually:
`L.control.attribution({ prefix: false }).addAttribution('© MapTiler')`
Free tiers (MapTiler, OpenFreeMap, etc.) often have request limits. For production, consider a paid plan or self-hosted tiles (e.g., via `tileserver-gl`, `t-rex`, or PMTiles).
Ensure the vector tiles cover the zoom range you need (`minzoom`/`maxzoom` in the style). If you need higher zooms, generate them or use a provider that offers them.
MapLibre GL JS v4+ expects style spec version 8. Older styles (Mapbox-style v7) may need minor edits (e.g., `source-layer` names).
Vector tiles are lightweight, but complex styles (many layers, heavy filters) can still tax the GPU. Test on target devices and consider simplifying the style if needed.

If you need offline, bundle the style JSON and tiles in a **PMTiles** file and serve it with the `pmtiles://` protocol (see the `maplibre-pmtiles-patterns` skill). The plugin works with that out of the box.
The plugin is built for MapLibre GL JS v2–v4. If you upgrade to a newer major version, check the plugin’s release notes for any breaking changes.
